en: The Bhikṣu Prātimokṣa Sūtra of the Four-Part Vinaya,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of the Later Qin dynasty.
I prostrate and pay homage to all Buddhas, as well as to the Dharma and the Saṃgha of bhikṣus.
Now I shall expound the Vinaya rules, so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time.
The precepts are like a boundless ocean; like jewels, one never tires of seeking them.
Those who wish to protect the noble wealth of the Dharma, assemble and listen as I speak.
To eliminate the four *pārājika* dharmas, And to extinguish the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* dharmas,
As well as the thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* dharmas— May the assembly gather and listen as I speak.
Vipaśyin, Śikhin, Viśvabhū, Krakucchanda, and...
Kanakamuni, Kāśyapa, and Śākyamuni—these World-Honored Ones of great virtue—have explained this matter for me.
Now I wish to explain it well; may all you worthy ones listen together.
Just as a person whose feet are injured is unable to travel anywhere, so it is with one who has violated the precepts: they cannot be born among gods or humans.
If one wishes to be born in the heavens or among human beings, [one must maintain the precepts].
One should always guard the feet of the precepts, never allowing them to be damaged.
Just as a driver entering a perilous path suffers the anxiety of losing a pin or breaking an axle, so it is with the violation of the precepts; at the time of death, one harbors fear.

Just as a person looking into a mirror feels joy or sorrow at their own beauty or ugliness, so it is with the recitation of the precepts: one feels grief or delight at their being kept whole or violated.
Just as two armies engage in battle, where the brave advance and the timid retreat;
The recitation of the precepts is likewise: from purity comes peace, from defilement comes fear.
Among all in the world, the king is supreme; among all flowing waters, the ocean is supreme;
among all the stars, the moon is supreme; among all holy ones, the Buddha is supreme.
Among all the various codes of discipline, the Sūtra of Precepts is supreme;
the Tathāgata established these prohibitions and recites them every half-month.
"Has the Saṃgha assembled?"
He replied, "The Saṃgha has assembled. [The other asked,] "Is it in harmony?"
He replied, "The assembly is harmonious.
[The Buddha asked,] "Has anyone who has not yet received full ordination departed?"
If there is someone present, they are sent out, and he replies:
"Those who have not yet received the full precepts have already left.
If there is no one present, he replies:
"In this assembly, there is no one who has not received full ordination.
"Have the bhikṣus who have not come declared their consent (*chanda*) and purity (*pariśuddhi*)?
Having completed the formal act according to the Dharma, he replied:
"Regarding the announcement of the *kṣānti* (consent): If there is none, he replies,
"There is no one here who has announced the *kṣānti*."
“Who sent the bhikṣuṇī to request instruction?
One who had received the bhikṣuṇī’s commission explained what had been said and replied,
“She requested instruction.”
If there are none present, he should reply:
"There are no nuns here who have come to request instruction. [The questioner asks:
"What is the Saṃgha doing now that it is in harmony?"
He replied, "The *karmavācanā* for the recitation of the precepts.
[Then he said: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
Today, on the fifteenth day, the Saṃgha recites the Prātimokṣa. If the time for the Saṃgha has arrived, may the Saṃgha, being patient and attentive, listen as we recite the Prātimokṣa in harmony.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*). Is the motion established?
If it is accomplished, answer:
"It is accomplished.
If it is not accomplished, answer: [It is not accomplished].
"It is not so. Venerable sirs!
I now wish to recite the Prātimokṣa precepts; listen attentively and reflect upon them well."
If you know yourself to have committed an offense, you should immediately confess it; if you have not committed an offense, remain silent.
By remaining silent, it is known that all the venerable ones are pure.
If someone else asks you, you should answer in the same manner.
Thus, if a bhikṣu among the assembly, when questioned up to three times, remembers having committed an offense yet does not confess it, he incurs the guilt of intentional lying;
for the Buddha has declared that intentional lying is a dharma that obstructs the Path.
If a bhikṣu remembers having committed an offense and desires to seek purification, he should perform confession;
through confession, one attains peace and happiness. "Venerable sirs!..."
I have already recited the introduction to the Prātimokṣa Sūtra.
Now I ask the Venerable Ones:
Are you pure in this regard?
The second and third times were also spoken in this manner:
"Venerable sirs! Since you are pure in this matter, as indicated by your silence, let it be so held."
"Venerable sirs!
These four *pārājika* dharmas are recited every half-month from within the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*. 'If a bhikṣu..."

If a bhikṣu, while sharing the same precepts as other bhikṣus, does not return his precepts, nor does he relinquish them when they have become weak, and yet commits an act of impurity— even with an animal—
this bhikṣu is defeated (pārājika) and shall not live in community.
"If a bhikṣu, whether in a village or in a secluded place, takes what is not given with a thieving mind—
according to the law regarding taking what is not given— if he is seized by a king or a royal minister, or is executed, bound, or driven out of the country: [he commits a pārājika offense]."
"You are a thief! You are deluded!
You possess no knowledge!"
"Such a bhikṣu commits a pārājika offense and shall not live in community.
If a bhikṣu intentionally takes the life of a human being with his own hand, provides a weapon to another, praises death, or encourages death, saying: [it would be better to die]..."
"Alas, man! What is the use of this wretched life?
It would be better to die than to live."
If he reflects in this manner and, through various means, praises death and encourages death as something pleasant,
that bhikṣu commits a pārājika offense and is not to live in community with the others.
"If a bhikṣu, while actually possessing no knowledge, claims of himself:
'I have attained the state of a superior man; I have entered the noble wisdom of the supreme Dharma; I know this; I see this. "
At a later time, whether questioned or unasked, desiring to purify himself, he speaks thus:
"I truly did not know and did not see, yet I said I knew and I saw; it was a false, deceptive, and lying speech."
"Excepting one who has overweening pride (*adhimāna*),
this bhikṣu has committed a *pārājika* offense and shall not live in communion. Venerable sirs!"
I have already explained the four *pārājika* rules.
If a bhikṣu commits any one of these *pārājika* offenses, he may not dwell together with the bhikṣus as before; it shall be the same hereafter.
This bhikṣu has committed a pārājika offense and should not dwell together [with the Saṃgha].
Now I ask the Venerable Ones:
Are you pure in this matter?
The second and third times were spoken in the same manner:
"Venerable sirs! Since you are silent, you are pure in this matter; let it be held thus."
"Venerable sirs!
These thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* dharmas are recited every half-month from within the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*. 'If a bhikṣu..."
Therefore, intentionally emitting semen, except in a dream, is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. "If a bhikṣu,
with a lustful mind, makes physical contact with a woman— whether grasping her hand or grasping her hair..."
If he touches any part of her body, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
"If a bhikṣu, with a lustful mind,
addresses a woman with coarse and lewd words of sexual desire, for whatever such coarse and lewd words of sexual desire he speaks, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*."
"If a bhikṣu, with lustful intent, in the presence of a woman, praises his own person,
saying: 'O great lady!'"

"I practice the holy life, maintaining the precepts with diligence and cultivating wholesome dharmas; you may offer this dharma of sexual desire to me, for such an offering is the foremost and most supreme."
“Saṃghāvaśeṣa. ‘If a bhikṣu acts as a go-between for others,
conveying a man’s intentions to a woman and a woman’s intentions to a man— whether for the purpose of formal marriage or for illicit intercourse— even for a mere moment, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa.’”
"If a bhikṣu seeks to build a house for himself, without an owner and for his own use, it must be built according to the prescribed measurements.
The measurement therein is: twelve spans of the Buddha’s hand in length, and seven spans in internal width."
When a monk intends to have another monk designate a site, that other monk shall point out a site that is free from difficulties and free from obstacles.

If a monk builds a hut for himself, without an owner, for his own use, on a site that has difficulties or obstacles, and does not have another monk designate the site, or if he builds it to excessive dimensions, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

"If a bhikṣu wishes to build a large dwelling for himself that has a patron, he should take other bhikṣus and go to point out the site; those bhikṣus should point out a site that is free from difficulties and free from obstructions."
If a bhikṣu constructs a large dwelling in a place that is dangerous or obstructed, for himself and with a patron, without having another bhikṣu point out the location, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
"If a bhikṣu, being overcome by anger,
should defame a bhikṣu who is not guilty of a pārājika offense with a groundless pārājika charge, desiring to destroy that person's pure conduct."
At a later time, whether questioned or unasked, if he knows that this matter was spoken without foundation and says,
"I spoke these words out of anger," if a bhikṣu makes such a statement, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
"If a bhikṣu, out of malice,

takes a fragment from a matter of a different category and, though the bhikṣu is not guilty of a pārājika offense, slanders him with a groundless pārājika charge, desiring to destroy his pure conduct."
At a later time, whether questioned or unasked, he knows that this was taken from a portion of a different matter;
that bhikṣu says of himself: "I spoke these words out of anger."
One who speaks these words commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
"If a bhikṣu, desiring to cause a schism in a harmonious Saṃgha, employs means to adopt the methods for causing a schism in a harmonious Saṃgha, and persists in them without relinquishing them..."
That bhikṣu should admonish this bhikṣu, saying: "Venerable sir! Do not cause a schism in the Saṃgha;
do not employ means to cause a schism in the Saṃgha; do not accept the principles that cause a schism and persist in them without relinquishing them."
"Venerable sir!

You should be in harmony with the Saṅgha, rejoicing and not disputing, studying under the same teacher as one body, like water mixed with milk; thus you will find increase and dwell in peace and happiness within the Buddha-dharma."
When that bhikṣu thus admonishes him and he persists in his refusal to relinquish it,
those bhikṣus should admonish him three times so that he may relinquish this matter, even unto the third admonition.
If he renounces it, it is well;
if he does not renounce it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. "If a bhikṣu..."
There are other companions, whether one, two, three, or even innumerable.
That bhikṣu says to those bhikṣus:
"Venerable sirs!..."
"Do not admonish this bhikṣu; this bhikṣu is one who speaks according to the Dharma and speaks according to the Vinaya.
What this bhikṣu says, we delight in; what this bhikṣu says, we approve of."
That bhikṣu said: "Venerable sirs!

Do not speak such words, saying that this bhikṣu is a bhikṣu who speaks according to the Dharma and a bhikṣu who speaks according to the Vinaya, and that we delight in what this bhikṣu says and we approve of what this bhikṣu says."
However, this bhikṣu is not one who speaks according to the Dharma, nor is he one who speaks according to the Vinaya.
Venerable sirs!
Do not seek to cause a schism in the Saṃgha; you should instead desire harmony within the Saṃgha.
"Venerable sir!

You should be in harmony with the Saṃgha, rejoicing and not disputing, studying under the same teacher as one body, like water and milk blending together; thus you shall find increase in the Buddha-dharma and dwell in peace and happiness."

When that bhikṣu thus admonishes him and he persists in his refusal to relinquish the matter, those bhikṣus should admonish him a third time so that he may relinquish it; this should be done up to three times.
"If he renounces it, it is well;
if he does not renounce it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. If a bhikṣu..."

Residing in dependence upon a village or a town, he defiles the families of others and engages in evil conduct; that he defiles the families of others and engages in evil conduct is both seen and heard.
The monks should say to that monk: "Venerable sir!
You have defiled a family and committed evil deeds; you have been seen and heard to have defiled a family, and you have been seen and heard to have committed evil deeds, Venerable sir!"
"You have defiled families and practiced evil conduct; you should now depart from this village and need not remain here.
When that bhikṣu spoke these words to the other bhikṣu, he replied:
"Venerable sir!..."
There are monks who possess attachment, aversion, fear, and delusion; thus, among monks who have committed the same offense, some are expelled while others are not.
The bhikṣus replied: "Venerable sir,
do not speak such words."
"There is lust, there is hatred, there is fear, and there is delusion; thus, among bhikṣus who have committed the same offense, some are expelled while others are not."
"Furthermore, the bhikṣus are not driven by affection, nor by hatred, nor by fear, nor by delusion.
Venerable Sir!
They defile families and engage in evil conduct; they are both seen and heard to defile families, and they are both seen and heard to engage in evil conduct."
When that bhikṣu thus admonishes him and he persists in his refusal to relinquish it,
those bhikṣus should admonish him three times so that he may relinquish this matter— up to the third admonition.
If he relinquishes it, it is well;
if he does not relinquish it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. "If a bhikṣu..."

Being of a wicked nature, he does not accept the words of others; when the bhikṣus have admonished him in accordance with the Dharma regarding the precepts, he himself does not accept their admonition, saying:
"Venerable sirs!..."
Do not speak to me of what is good or bad, nor shall I speak to you, venerable sirs, of what is good or bad.
Venerable sirs, please desist!
"Do not admonish me.
That bhikṣu should then admonish this bhikṣu, saying:
"Venerable sir!..."

Do not yourself refuse to accept admonition; Venerable Sir, you should yourself accept admonition. Just as the Venerable Sir admonishes the bhikṣus in accordance with the Dharma, so too should the bhikṣus admonish the Venerable Sir in accordance with the Dharma.
"In this way, the community of the Buddha’s disciples will attain increase, admonishing one another, instructing one another, and confessing to one another.
When that bhikṣu thus receives such admonition and yet persists firmly without relinquishing his position,
those bhikṣus should admonish him three times so that he may abandon this matter, continuing until the third admonition.
"It is well if he relinquishes it;
if he does not relinquish it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. Venerable sirs!"
I have already explained the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* dharmas: nine are offenses upon first commission, and four require up to three admonitions.
If a bhikṣu commits any one of these dharmas and knowingly conceals it, he should be compelled to undergo *parivāsa*;
once the *parivāsa* is completed, he should further be granted six nights of *mānatva*.
Once the *mānatva* has been performed, there remains the matter of the removal of the offense (*āpattivyutthāna*).

This bhikṣu’s offense must be removed within a saṃgha of twenty monks; if even one person is missing and the assembly does not reach twenty, the bhikṣu’s offense cannot be removed, and the other bhikṣus may also censure him. This is the proper time for this.
Now I ask the venerable ones:
Are you pure in this matter?
Thus it is asked three times.
"Venerable sirs! Since there is silence, you are pure in this matter; thus it shall be held. Venerable sirs!"
These two indeterminate rules are recited every half-month from within the *Prātimokṣa* Sūtra:
"If a bhikṣu sits alone with a woman in a secluded, concealed, or screened place— a place suitable for sexual intercourse— and speaks improper words."
There was a laywoman follower established in faith who, regarding each of three matters—
whether it be a *pārājika*, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, or a *pāyattika*— spoke thus to the bhikṣu sitting there:
"The bhikṣu himself has said this:"
"I have committed this offense.
Regarding these three categories of dharma, he should be dealt with one by one:

whether it be a *pārājika*, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, or a *pāyattika*. As stated by a laywoman (*upāsikā*) who is established in faith, that bhikṣu should be disciplined according to the law; this is called an *aniyata* dharma.
"If a bhikṣu, together with a woman, sits in an exposed place, an improper place for sexual intercourse, and utters coarse and wicked words;
and if a faithful upāsikā states one or another of two dharmas: [he has committed an offense]."
Whether it be a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* or a *pāyattika*,
if the monk sitting there says of himself:
"I have committed this offense."
"Regarding these two categories of offenses, each should be dealt with according to its specific rule:

whether it be a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* or a *pāyattika*, one should deal with that bhikṣu according to the law as stated by the laywoman (*upāsikā*) who is endowed with faith. This is called an indeterminate rule (*aniyata-dharma*)."
"Venerable sirs! I have already recited the two *aniyata* dharmas.
Now I ask the venerable sirs: [Is it pure in this matter?]"
"Are you pure in this matter?
Thus it is asked three times, O Venerable Ones!
Since there is silence, you are pure in this matter; thus shall this be held."
"Venerable sirs!
These thirty *niḥsargika-pāyattika* dharmas are recited every half-month from within the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*.
'If a bhikṣu..."

When the robes have been finished and the *kaṭhina* robe has been withdrawn, one may keep an extra robe for ten days; it may be kept provided it has not been formally assigned as "impure. If it exceeds ten days, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.

"If a bhikṣu, when his robes are finished and the kaṭhina has been relinquished, should stay overnight apart from any one of his three robes in a different location, except by formal authorization of the Saṃgha (saṃgha-kamma), it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (niḥsargika-pāyattika)."

“Monks, when the robes have been finished and the kaṭhina privileges have been relinquished, if a monk obtains an out-of-season robe and wishes to accept it, he may do so; having accepted it, he must quickly have it made into a robe. If it is sufficient, that is well;
if it is not sufficient, he may keep it for one month in order to complete it.”
If one keeps it beyond that limit, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu should receive a robe from a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, except in exchange for trade, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣu should have a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative wash an old robe, or dye it, or beat it, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*. "If a bhikṣu..."
If a bhikṣu asks for a robe from a householder or a householder’s wife who is not a relative, except at the appropriate times, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
The "appropriate times" are when a bhikṣu has had his robes taken away, lost his robes, had his robes burned, or had his robes carried away by water; these are called the appropriate times.
"If a bhikṣu has lost his robes,

had them stolen, burned them, or had them carried away by water, and a householder or householder’s wife who is not a relative should of their own accord invite him and offer many robes, that bhikṣu should receive the robes with contentment."
If one accepts more than this, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

"If a bhikṣu, when a householder or a householder’s wife has prepared the price for a robe for a bhikṣu, intending to purchase such a robe to give to a certain bhikṣu, goes to that householder’s home before having been invited by him and says:..."
“Excellent, householder!
Buy such and such a robe for me and give it to me, so that it may be fine.
If she obtains the robe, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
“If, monks, two householders or two housewives provide the price for a robe for a monk, intending to purchase such a robe with that price and give it to a certain monk;”
This bhikṣu, without having previously received a formal invitation from a householder, goes to the homes of two householders and speaks as follows:
"Excellent, householders!"
"Provide such and such an amount for the price of robes so that we may make one robe together for the sake of excellence.
If she obtains a robe [in this manner], it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

"If a bhikṣu, when a king, a great minister, a brahmin, a householder, or a householder’s wife sends a messenger to deliver the price for a robe, saying: 'Take this price for a robe and give it to such-and-such a bhikṣu.'"
That messenger went to where the bhikṣu was and said to him:
"Venerable sir!
For your sake, I have sent this price for robes; please accept it."
That bhikṣu should speak thus to the messenger:
"I should not accept this price for robes; if I need a robe, I shall accept one that is appropriate for the season and pure."
The messenger said to the bhikṣu:
"Venerable sir!
Are there any attendants?"
The bhikṣu who needs robes should say:
"There are! Whether they be monastery attendants or upāsakas, these are the attendants for the bhikṣus who constantly perform services for them."
Then that messenger went to the person in charge, gave him the price for the robe, and returned to where the bhikṣu was, speaking thus:
"Venerable Sir!..."
"Regarding the attendant whom you have designated, I have already given him the price for the robe. Venerable sir!
You should know the time; go there and you shall receive the robe.
The bhikṣu who requires a robe should go to the place where the attendant is and, after reminding him a second or third time, should say:
"I need a robe. If he reminds him thus two or three times and obtains the robe, that is well;
if he does not obtain the robe, he should stand silently before him four, five, or six times, so as to cause him to remember.
If he stands silently before [the donor] four times, five times, or six times, it is well if he obtains the robe;
if he does not obtain the robe, and he obtains it by seeking beyond that, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If he does not obtain the robe, he should go to the place where the price for the robe was received, either in person or by sending a messenger, and say:

"Previously you sent a messenger with the price for a robe to a certain bhikṣu; that bhikṣu did not ultimately receive the robe. You should take it back so that it is not lost; this is the proper time. (10)
"If a bhikṣu makes a new bedding out of mixed wild silk-cotton, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*. If a bhikṣu..."
If one makes a new bedding using pure black wool from a newly shorn sheep, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu makes a new bedding,
he should use two parts of pure black wool, three parts of white, and four parts of variegated wool."
If a bhikṣu makes a new bedding without using two parts black, three parts white, and four parts variegated, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (niḥsargika-pāyattika).
"If a bhikṣu makes a new bedding or mat, he must use it for six years. If it has not yet reached six years,
and he does not discard the old one to make another new one— except by formal authorization from the Saṃgha— he commits an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (niḥsargika-pāyattika)."
"If a bhikṣu makes a new sitting mat,
he must take a piece from an old one, measuring one span in length and breadth, and patch it onto the new one in order to spoil its color."

If one makes a new sitting mat and does not take a piece from an old one, measuring at least one span in length and breadth, to be attached to the surface of the new one for the purpose of discoloring it, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
“If a bhikṣu, while traveling on a road,
obtains wool and there is no one to carry it, he may carry it himself for up to three yojanas.
If there is no one to carry it and he carries it himself beyond three yojanas, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.”
"If a bhikṣu should have a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative wash, dye, or card wool, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*. If a bhikṣu..."
If a bhikṣu takes money, gold, or silver with his own hand,
or instructs another to take it, or accepts it when it has been placed on the ground, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (niḥsargika-pāyattika). "If a bhikṣu..."
If a bhikṣu engages in various kinds of buying and selling of precious objects,
it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu engages in various kinds of trade, it is the twentieth *niḥsargika-pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣu keeps an extra alms-bowl without having made it a formal gift, he may do so for up to ten days.
If he exceeds this period, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (niḥsargika-pāyattika)."

"If a bhikṣu possesses a bowl that has fewer than five patches and is not leaking, yet seeks a new bowl for the sake of its appearance, and should he obtain one, it is a niḥsargika-pāyattika offense."
That bhikṣu should go before the Saṃgha to relinquish it; the bowls should be passed around one by one until the very lowest bowl is selected and given to him to keep.
He should continue to keep it until it breaks; this is the proper occasion.
"If a bhikṣu himself begs for thread and has a weaver who is not a relative weave it into a robe for him, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*. If a bhikṣu..."
A layman or a laywoman has a weaver weave a robe for a bhikṣu.
Before having been invited by a formal request, that bhikṣu goes to the weaver’s place and says:
"This robe is being made for me; weave it for me very well, making it wide, large, and firm, and I shall give you some small amount of payment."
If a bhikṣu gives the price—even as much as the value of a single meal—and obtains a robe, it is a niḥsargika-pāyattika. "If a bhikṣu..."
Having first given a robe to a bhikṣu, he later, out of anger, either seizes it himself or instructs another to seize it, saying:
"Give me back my robe; I will not give it to you."
If a bhikṣu returns his robe and the one who takes that robe [does so], it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu has an illness,
he may consume the remaining medicinal substances— clarified butter, oil, fresh butter, honey, and rock sugar— for up to seven days."
If one wears it for more than seven days, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu, when there remains one month of the spring season, seeks a rain-bath robe, he should use it for bathing for half a month."
"If a bhikṣu seeks a rain-bath robe more than one month in advance, or uses it for bathing more than half a month in advance, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. If a bhikṣu..."
Within ten days before the end of the three months of the summer retreat, the bhikṣus may receive robes offered as urgent gifts.
Knowing that these are robes offered as urgent gifts, the bhikṣus should accept them.
Having accepted them, they may keep them until the time for the distribution of robes.
If one keeps them beyond this limit, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*. "If a bhikṣu,

at the end of the three months of the summer retreat, when the month of Kārttika has been completed, should dwell in an araṇya that is a place of suspected danger and fear, and while dwelling in such a place, should wish to leave any one of his three robes behind in a village dwelling, those bhikṣus may, for a valid reason, be separated from their robes for up to six nights."
If one exceeds [the limit], it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. "If a bhikṣu,
knowing it to be property belonging to the Saṃgha, seeks to appropriate it for himself, it is the thirtieth *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*."
"Venerable sirs!
I have already recited the thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* dharmas.
Now I ask the venerable sirs: [Is this dharma pure?]"
"Are you pure in this matter?
Thus it is asked three times, O Venerable Ones!
Since there is silence, you are pure in this matter; thus shall this be held."
"Venerable sirs!
These ninety *pāyattika* dharmas are recited every half-month from within the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*.
'If a bhikṣu..."
"To speak falsely with full knowledge is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu speaks words that disparage another by their class [or lineage], it is a *pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣu speaks with double-tongued speech, it is a pāyattika. If a bhikṣu..."
"To sleep in the same room as a woman, it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu sleeps together with one who has not received the full ordination, exceeding two nights and reaching a third night, it is a *pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣu recites the Dharma together with a person who has not received full ordination,
it is a pāyattika. If a bhikṣu..."

If a bhikṣu knows that another bhikṣu has committed a grave offense and speaks of it to one who has not received full ordination, except by formal authorization of the Saṃgha, it is a pāyattika. "If a bhikṣu..."
If one speaks of superhuman states (uttari-manuṣya-dharma) to a person who has not yet received the full ordination (upasaṃpadā), saying, "I have seen this;
I know this," and it is true, it is a pāyattika offense.
"If a bhikṣu should preach the Dharma to a woman for more than five or six sentences, except when a man capable of understanding is present,
it is a pāyattika. If a bhikṣu..."
If a bhikṣu digs the earth with his own hands, or instructs another to dig it, it is a pāyattika offense, number ten.
"If a bhikṣu destroys a village of spirits (yakṣagrāma), it is a pāyattika offense."
"If a bhikṣu should speak falsely and with ulterior motives to annoy another,
it is a pāyattika. "If a bhikṣu..."
If one reviles or scolds [another], it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu takes a monastic corded bed,

a wooden bed, or bedding or a mat, spreads it in the open air, or instructs another to spread it, and then departs without putting it away himself or instructing another to put it away, it is a *pāyattika*."

"If a bhikṣu, within a monastic dwelling, spreads bedding belonging to the Saṃgha— whether spreading it himself or instructing another to spread it— and then sits or lies upon it, yet when departing does not himself remove it nor instruct another to remove it, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that another bhikṣu already occupies a dwelling, comes later and forcibly spreads out bedding within it to stay the night, thinking:
'If he finds it cramped, he will naturally move away from me.'"
If one acts with such a motive and for no other reason, and it is not due to [proper] deportment,
it is a *pāyattika*. "If a bhikṣu,
being angry with another bhikṣu and displeased with him, personally drags him out of a communal dwelling (*saṃghārāma*), or instructs another to drag him out, it is a *pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣu, in a room or on an upper story of a multi-storied building, sits or lies down upon a rope bed or a wooden bed with detachable legs, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that water contains living beings, pours it onto mud or grass, or instructs another to pour it, he commits a pāyattika offense. "If a bhikṣu..."

If one constructs a large dwelling, including its doors, windows, and other decorative furnishings, and directs that the thatching be applied in two or three layers—if it exceeds this, it is the twentieth *pāyattika* offense.
"If a bhikṣu, without being appointed by the Saṃgha, instructs a bhikṣuṇī,
it is a pāyattika. If a bhikṣu..."
If one has been appointed by the Saṃgha to instruct bhikṣuṇīs and continues until sunset,
it is a pāyattika. "If a bhikṣu speaks to another bhikṣu, saying:..."
"If a bhikṣu, for the sake of food or drink, instructs a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣu gives a robe to a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, except in exchange, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu makes a robe for a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, it is a pāyattika. If a bhikṣu..."
"To sit in a secluded place with a bhikṣuṇī constitutes a pāyattika offense. Furthermore,
if a bhikṣu makes an appointment with a bhikṣuṇī to travel along the same road together, from one village to another village, except at other times, it constitutes a pāyattika offense."
"An unusual time" refers to when one travels with merchants, or when there is suspicion, fear, or terror;
this is called an unusual time.
"If a bhikṣu makes an appointment with a bhikṣuṇī to ride together in the same boat, whether going upriver or downriver—with the exception of crossing directly across—he commits a pāyattika offense."

"If a bhikṣu, knowing that food was obtained through the cause of a bhikṣuṇī's praise and exhortation, should eat it— except when there was a prior intention on the part of the donor— it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu makes an appointment with a woman to travel along the same road, even as far as the distance between two villages, it is a *pāyattika* offense,
number thirty. If a bhikṣu..."
"At a place where a single meal is offered, a bhikṣu who is not ill should eat only one meal; if he receives more than that, it is a pāyattika offense.
'If a bhikṣu eats from one [donor] to another (successive eating), except at other times, it is a pāyattika offense.'"
"Other times" refers to the time of illness and the time of receiving robes; these are called "other times.
"If a bhikṣu eats separately from the community, except at other times, it is a pāyattika offense."

The exceptions are: when one is ill, when making robes, when robes are being offered, when traveling on a road, when traveling by boat, when a great assembly has gathered, and when śramaṇas are distributing food; these are the appropriate times.

“If a bhikṣu goes to the home of a layperson and is invited by them to receive cakes, parched grain, or boiled rice, and that bhikṣu wishes to accept it, he may accept two or three bowls. Upon returning to the saṃghārāma, he should divide it and give it to the other bhikṣus to eat.”
If a bhikṣu who is not ill accepts more than two or three bowls of food and, upon returning to the monastery, does not share it with other bhikṣus, it is a pāyattika offense.
"If a bhikṣu, having finished his meal,
should at some time accept an invitation and eat without performing the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta* (remaining-food) procedure,
it is a *pāyattika*. "If a bhikṣu..."
Knowing that another bhikṣu has already finished his meal, if one accepts an invitation and, without performing the ritual for leftover food, earnestly invites him to eat, saying:
"Venerable sir!
Take this food."
For this reason, and no other, if one intends to cause another to commit an offense,
it is a *pāyattika*. "If a bhikṣu eats food at an improper time, it is a *pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣu eats food that has been kept overnight, it is a pāyattika. If a bhikṣu..."
"If one receives food that has not been formally offered, or places medicine in the mouth— excluding water and tooth-sticks— it is a *pāyattika*.
'If a bhikṣu obtains fine and delicious food, such as milk, curd, fish, or meat, and if that bhikṣu, being without illness, seeks such fine food for his own sake, it is the fortieth *pāyattika*.'"
"If a bhikṣu gives food with his own hand to a male follower of another sect or a female follower of another sect,
it is a pāyattika. If a bhikṣu..."

Having previously accepted an invitation, if one visits other households for a meal before or after the designated time without having informed another bhikṣu—except during the special times—it is a pāyattika offense.
"Other times" refers to the time of illness, the time of making robes, and the time of receiving robes; these are called "other times.
"If a bhikṣu, while in a household where there is wealth, sits down forcefully, it is a pāyattika offense."
"If a bhikṣu sits in a secluded place within a household where there are valuables,
it is a pāyattika. If a bhikṣu..."
If a bhikṣu sits alone with a woman on exposed ground, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu says to another bhikṣu: [as follows]..."
"Venerable sir!
Let us go together to the village; I shall give you food there.
Yet that bhikṣu ultimately did not instruct [the other] to give food to this bhikṣu, but said:
"Go! I do not find pleasure in sitting or speaking with you; I find pleasure in sitting and speaking alone.
If, for this reason and no other, one uses such a means to send [the person] away, it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu is invited to receive medicine for four months, a bhikṣu who is not ill should accept it;

if he accepts it beyond that period—except in the case of a regular invitation, a renewed invitation, a partial invitation, or a lifelong invitation—it is a pāyattika. If a bhikṣu goes to view an army formation, except when there is a specific reason, it is a pāyattika."
“If a bhikṣu, for a valid reason, is permitted to stay within an army for two or three nights; if he exceeds this, it is a pāyattika. If a bhikṣu...”

If one stays within an army for two or three nights, or at times observes military formations and battles, or observes the strength and power of the troops' elephants and horses, it is a *pāyattika* offense, number fifty.
"If a bhikṣu drinks alcohol, it is a pāyattika. If a bhikṣu..."
"To sport in water, it is a *pāyattika*.
'If a bhikṣu strikes or tickles another with his fingers, it is a *pāyattika*.'"
"If a bhikṣu does not accept admonition, it is a pāyattika. If a bhikṣu..."
"To frighten another bhikṣu is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣu bathes once every half-month, a bhikṣu who is not ill should accept this [rule]; he must not exceed it, except at other times, for which there is a pāyattika."
"Other times" refers to:
the time of heat, the time of illness, the time of work, the time of wind, the time of rain, and the time of traveling on a road;
these are the other times. "If a bhikṣu..."

If a bhikṣu, being free from illness, lights a fire or instructs another to light one on the open ground for the sake of warming his own body, except when there is a specific reason or occasion, it is a pāyattika offense. "If a bhikṣu..."
If one conceals another bhikṣu’s robe, alms bowl, sitting mat, or needle case—whether concealing them oneself or instructing another to do so—even down to doing so in jest, it is a pāyattika offense.
"If a bhikṣu gives a robe to a bhikṣu,
a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, and later takes it back and wears it without informing the owner, it is a pāyattika."
“If a bhikṣu obtains a new robe,
he should apply one of three types of discoloration, choosing whichever he prefers from among blue, black, or madder-brown.”
If a bhikṣu wears any other new robe without having dyed it with one of the three types of disfiguring colors— whether blue, black, or madder— it is a pāyattika offense, number sixty.
"If a bhikṣu intentionally kills the life of an animal, it is a pāyattika. If a bhikṣu..."
If a bhikṣu knowingly drinks or uses water containing living beings,
it is a pāyattika. "If a bhikṣu intentionally annoys another bhikṣu so as to cause him even a moment of unhappiness, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that another bhikṣu has committed a grave offense (sthūlātyaya), conceals it,
he commits a pāyattika. If a bhikṣu..."
If one knows that a person is less than twenty years of age and yet confers the full precepts upon them, this person does not obtain the precepts;
that bhikṣu is to be censured for his folly, and it is a pāyattika offense.
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that a matter of dispute has been settled according to the Dharma through confession, should later raise it again,
it is a pāyattika. If a bhikṣu..."

If one knows they are traveling companions of thieves, makes an agreement with them, and travels along the same path together for even as far as the distance between two villages, it is a *pāyattika*. "If a bhikṣu..."
He speaks thus: "I know the Dharma taught by the Buddha; engaging in sexual intercourse is not a dharma that obstructs the path.
That monk should admonish this monk, saying:

"Venerable Sir! Do not speak such words; do not slander the World-Honored One. It is unwholesome to slander the World-Honored One. The World-Honored One does not speak thus. By means of countless skillful expedients, the World-Honored One has taught that engaging in sexual desire is a dharma that obstructs the Path."
When that bhikṣu exhorts this bhikṣu, if he persists and does not relinquish [his position], that bhikṣu may exhort him up to three times.
For the sake of making him relinquish this matter, if he relinquishes it upon the third exhortation, it is well; if he does not relinquish it, it is a pāyattika offense.

"If a bhikṣu, knowing that a person who speaks such words has not yet performed the formal act, and knowing that they do not relinquish such wrong views, provides them with what they require, performs karmavācanā together with them, or stays and converses with them, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu knows that a śrāmaṇera has spoken thus:
'I have heard from the Buddha that engaging in sexual intercourse is not an obstacle to the path.'"
That bhikṣu should admonish that śrāmaṇera, saying:
"Do not slander the Blessed One; it is unwholesome to slander the Blessed One.
The Blessed One does not speak such words."
"Śrāmaṇera! The World-Honored One has, through countless skillful means, declared that sexual desire is a dharma that obstructs the Path.
When that bhikṣu exhorted this śrāmaṇera in this way, he stubbornly clung to his position and would not relinquish it.

That bhikṣu should admonish and exhort him up to two or three times so that he may abandon this matter. If he abandons it after being exhorted up to three times, that is well; if he does not abandon it, that bhikṣu should say to this śrāmaṇera:

"From this day forward, you must no longer say, 'The Buddha is my World-Honored One,' nor may you follow other bhikṣus. While other śrāmaṇeras are permitted to stay with bhikṣus for two or three nights, you no longer have such a privilege. You must leave! Depart! You should not remain here."

If a bhikṣu, knowing that a śrāmaṇera has been expelled from such a community, yet entices him away, keeps him as a follower, dwells with him, or converses with him, it is a pāyattika offense, number seventy.
"If a bhikṣu, when other bhikṣus are admonishing him in accordance with the Dharma, speaks thus:
'I will not train in this precept now.'"
If one should challenge or question other wise bhikṣus who uphold the Vinaya, it is a pāyattika offense.
However, if it is for the purpose of seeking knowledge or for the sake of study, one may challenge or question them. "If a bhikṣu..."
At the time of reciting the precepts, he spoke these words:
"Venerable Sirs!
What is the use of reciting these minor and trivial rules?"
"When this precept is being recited, it causes people to feel distressed, ashamed, or doubtful.
Because of thus disparaging the precepts, it is a *pāyattika* offense. "If a bhikṣu..."
When the recitation of the precepts takes place, one speaks these words:
"I have only now come to know this rule, which is recorded in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* and has been proclaimed every half-month from within the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*."
If other bhikṣus know that this bhikṣu has sat through two or three recitations of the *Poṣadha*— let alone more— and yet he remains ignorant and lacks understanding,
then if he commits an offense, he should be dealt with according to the Dharma, and furthermore, a heavier penalty for ignorance shall be added.
He said: "Elder! You have gained no benefit; you have not attained it well."
"When you recite the precepts, you do not apply your mind or listen attentively with a focused ear.
Because of that ignorance, it is a *pāyattika*. "If a bhikṣu..."
After the communal *karmavācanā* has been performed, if one speaks thus:
"O Bhikṣus, give the property of the Saṃgha to those with whom you have a close or intimate relationship," it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu, while the Saṃgha’s deliberation on a matter is not yet concluded, rises and departs without having given his consent (chanda),
it is a pāyattika. If a bhikṣu..."
If, having already given one's consent, one later regrets it,
it is a *pāyattika*. "If a bhikṣu,
after bhikṣus have engaged in a quarrel, listens to these words and reports them to the other side, it is a *pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣu, out of anger and displeasure, strikes another bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika. If a bhikṣu..."
If, out of anger and displeasure, one strikes a bhikṣu with the hand, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu, out of anger,
slanders another with a groundless saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, it is the eightieth pāyattika."
“If a bhikṣu enters the palace of a Kṣatriya king of the ‘water-sprinkled head’ lineage while the king has not yet gone out and the treasures have not yet been stored away,
and he crosses the threshold of the palace gate, it is a pāyattika.”
"If a bhikṣu, whether it be gems or gem-ornaments, takes them up himself or causes another to take them up, except within a monastery or a lodging place, it is a pāyattika."

If a bhikṣu, while in a monastery or at a lodging place, takes hold of a jewel or an ornament made of jewels—whether taking it up himself or instructing another to take it—he should form this thought:
"If there is an owner who recognizes it, they shall take it."
"Such is the causal basis, and not otherwise:
'If a bhikṣu enters a village at an improper time without having informed another bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika.'"

"If a bhikṣu makes a corded bed or a wooden bed, the legs should be no higher than eight finger-breadths of the Tathāgata, excluding the portion inserted into the mortise holes at the top; if they exceed this, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu makes a cotton-wool mattress for a corded bed, a wooden bed, or a large or small mat, and it is completed,
it is a pāyattika. If a bhikṣu..."
If one makes a needle case from bone, ivory, or horn, having carved or scraped it out, it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu makes a *niṣīdana*,
he should make it according to the prescribed measure."

Regarding the measurements herein: the length shall be two spans of the Buddha’s hand, and the width one and a half spans. If the length or width is increased by more than half a span each, or if it exceeds these limits after being finished, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
"If a bhikṣu makes a cloth for covering sores, it must be made according to the prescribed measure. The measure herein is:
four spans of the Buddha’s hand in length and two spans in width. If, having finished cutting it, it exceeds these dimensions, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu makes a rain-bath robe, it must be made according to the prescribed measurements. The measurement therein is:
six spans of the Buddha’s hand in length and two and a half spans in width. If it exceeds these, it must be cut down; [otherwise] it is a pāyattika offense."
"If a bhikṣu makes a robe equal in measure to that of the Tathāgata, or makes one exceeding that measure, it is a pāyattika.
Herein, the measure of the Tathāgata’s robe is nine spans of the Buddha’s hand in length and six spans in width; this is called the ninety-fold measure of the Tathāgata’s robe."
"Venerable sirs!
I have already recited the ninety *pāyattika* dharmas.
Now I ask the venerable sirs: [Are you pure in this matter?]"
"Is there purity herein?
Thus it is asked three times, O Venerable Ones!
Since there is silence, there is purity herein. This matter is thus upheld."
"Venerable sirs!
These four *pāṭidesanīya* dharmas are recited every half-month from within the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*.
'If a bhikṣu..."

If a bhikṣu enters a village and, being free from illness, takes food with his own hand from a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative and eats it, that bhikṣu should confess his transgression to another bhikṣu, saying:
"Venerable sir!..."
"I have committed a censurable offense, which I should not have done; I now repent before the Venerable One.
This is called the method of repentance. "If a bhikṣu..."
When eating at the home of a layperson, if there is a bhikṣuṇī therein who directs, saying, "Give such-and-such a person soup;
give such-and-such a person rice," that bhikṣu should speak to that bhikṣuṇī as follows: "Sister!..."
"Wait, we must wait until the bhikṣus have finished eating.
If not even a single bhikṣu says this to that bhikṣuṇī: "Sister!..."
"Stop for now; wait until the other bhikṣus have finished eating.
That bhikṣu should confess his transgression to another bhikṣu, saying:
"Venerable sir!"
"I have committed a blameworthy act, which I ought not to have done; I now repent before the Venerable One.
This is called the rite of repentance.

"If a *kula-kamma* (formal act regarding a family) has previously been performed, and if a bhikṣu, at such a family, accepts food with his own hands and eats it without prior invitation and while not being ill, that bhikṣu should repent before another bhikṣu, saying:"
"Venerable Sir!
I have committed a censurable offense, which ought not to have been done; I now repent before the Venerable Sir.
This is called the method of repentance.
"If a bhikṣu dwells in an araṇya,
a remote and desolate place where there is suspicion and fear,
and while dwelling in such an araṇya, that bhikṣu has not previously informed a donor that he will not accept food outside the monastery grounds."
If, within a monastery, a bhikṣu who is not ill receives food with his own hand and eats it, he should confess his transgression to another bhikṣu, saying:
"Venerable sir!..."
"I have committed a censurable offense, which I ought not to have done; I now repent before the Venerable Ones.
This is called the rite of repentance.
"Venerable Ones!..."
I have already recited the four *pāṭidesanīya* dharmas.
Now I ask the venerable ones:
Are you pure in this regard?
Thus, Venerable Ones, have I asked three times.
Since there is silence, you are pure in this matter; thus shall it be held. "Venerable Ones!"
These rules of training for the community are recited every half-month from within the Sūtra of Precepts:
"One should train oneself to wear the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* properly and neatly."
"One should train oneself: 'I shall wear the three robes in a neat and orderly manner.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not walk into the house of a layperson with my robe tucked over one shoulder.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not sit down in the house of a layperson with my robe tucked over one shoulder.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter the house of a layperson with my robe wrapped around my neck.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not sit in the house of a layperson with my robe wrapped around my neck.'"
"One should train oneself: 'One must not enter the house of a layperson with one's head covered.
One should train oneself: 'One must not sit in the house of a layperson with one's head covered.
One should train oneself: 'One must not enter the house of a layperson by jumping.'"
"One should train oneself: 'One must not skip rows to enter the house of a layperson and sit.
One should train oneself: 'One must not squat while inside the house of a layperson.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not walk into the house of a layperson with hands crossed over my hips.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not sit in the house of a layperson with hands crossed over my hips.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter the house of a layperson while swaying the body.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not sit in the house of a layperson while swaying the body.'"
"One should train oneself: 'One must not walk with swinging arms into the house of a layperson.
One should train oneself: 'One must not sit with swinging arms in the house of a layperson.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall enter the homes of laypeople with my body well-covered.

"One should train oneself: 'I shall enter the house of a layperson in silence.

"Venerable sirs! I have now recited the rules of training for the community."
Now I ask the venerable ones:
Are you pure in this matter?
Thus it is asked three times, venerable ones!
"In this matter, we are pure, for we remain silent; thus shall this matter be upheld.
"Venerable sirs! These seven principles for settling disputes are recited every half-month from within the Sūtra of the Precepts."

Where the *smṛtivinaya* (settlement by recollection) is appropriate, one should grant the *smṛtivinaya*."
"Where the *amūḍhavinaya* (verdict for one who was not insane) should be granted, the *amūḍhavinaya* shall be granted.
Where the *pratijñākāraka* (verdict by confession) should be granted, the *pratijñākāraka* shall be granted.

"Venerable sirs! I have already recited the seven rules for settling disputes.

"O Venerable Ones!"

I have already recited the introduction to the Prātimokṣa Sūtra; I have already recited the four pārājika rules; I have already recited the thirteen saṃghāvaśeṣa rules; I have already recited the two aniyata rules; I have already recited the thirty naiḥsargika-pāyattika rules; I have already recited the ninety pāyattika rules; I have already recited the four pratideśanīya rules; I have already recited the śaikṣa training rules; and I have already recited the seven adhikaraṇa-śamatha rules. This is the Prātimokṣa Sūtra spoken by the Buddha, which is recited every half-month from within the Prātimokṣa Sūtra.
“If there are any other qualities of a Buddha, one should study them all together in harmony.
Patience is the supreme path; the Buddha has declared that the unconditioned is foremost.
One who causes affliction to others while claiming to have left the household life is not called a śramaṇa.”
"This is the Sīla-vagga (Discourse on Precepts) spoken by the Tathāgata Vipaśyin, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha:
'Just as a person with clear vision Can avoid dangerous and evil paths,
So too, in this world, a wise person Is able to distance themselves from all evils.'"
“This is the *Śīlaskandha-sūtra* spoken by the Tathāgata Śikhin, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha:
‘Do not revile, nor be envious; One should practice the precepts with devotion.
Know moderation in eating and drinking, And always delight in dwelling in solitude.’”
“With a concentrated mind, delighting in diligence—this is called the teaching of all Buddhas.
This is the precept scripture spoken by the Tathāgata Vipaśyin, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
"Just as a bee gathers from a flower, Without harming its color or fragrance,
but taking only its nectar to depart— so it is with a bhikṣu entering a village.
He does not interfere with others' affairs, nor does he observe what has been done or left undone."
"But observe your own conduct, whether it be right or wrong.
This is the precept discourse spoken by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha Krakucchanda.
"Do not be negligent in mind; you should diligently train in the noble Dharma.
Thus, free from sorrow, with a concentrated mind, you shall enter Nirvana.
This is the precept scripture spoken by the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kanakamuni.
"Do no evil in any way; Practice all that is good;
Purify your own mind— This is the teaching of all Buddhas.
This is the *Dharmapada* (Sutta on the Verses of the Law) spoken by the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kāśyapa.
"Guard well your speech, purify your own mind,
and let your body commit no evil; these three paths of action being pure—
able to practice in this way is the path of the Great Sages."
"This is the Sūtra of the Precepts spoken by the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, for the community of monks free from worldly affairs over the course of twelve years."
From this point forward, it shall be explained in detail.
Those bhikṣus who delight in the Dharma, who delight in the life of a śramaṇa, who possess a sense of shame and dread of blame, and who delight in training in the precepts, should train therein.
The wise person who can guard the precepts Will obtain three kinds of happiness:
Renown and material gain, And upon death, birth in the heavens.
One should contemplate such states; The wise should diligently guard the precepts.
With purity of precepts and wisdom, one attains the foremost path.
Just as the Buddhas of the past, those of the future,
and the World-Honored Ones of the present, are able to overcome all sorrow.
All together one should revere and honor the precepts; this is the Dharma of all Buddhas.
If there are those who act for their own sake and wish to seek the Buddha-way, they should respect the True Dharma; this is the teaching of all Buddhas.
The Seven Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, who have extinguished all fetters and defilements, have preached this Sūtra of the Seven Precepts; thereby all bonds are liberated.
Having entered into Nirvāṇa, all worldly play has been forever extinguished.
The Great Seer, the World-Honored One, has proclaimed the precepts praised by the noble sages;
these are the practices of his disciples, leading them into the stillness of nirvāṇa.
When the World-Honored One was about to enter nirvāṇa, he gave rise to great compassion.
Having assembled the community of bhikṣus, he gave them this instruction:
"Do not say that with my parinirvāṇa, those who practice purity will be without protection.
I now proclaim the Sūtra of Precepts and have also well expounded the Vinaya."
Although I have entered parinirvāṇa, you should regard this sutra as the World-Honored One;
as long as this sutra abides in the world, the Buddha-dharma will flourish.
Because it flourishes in this way, one shall attain entry into nirvāṇa.
If one does not uphold these precepts as they should be observed during the poṣadha, it is like the time when the sun sets: the world is entirely shrouded in darkness.
One should guard and uphold these precepts, just as a yak cherishes its tail.
Gathered together in one place, seated as the Buddha has taught:
I have recited the Prātimokṣa Sūtra, and the Saṃgha’s Poṣadha ceremony is concluded.
Regarding the merits spoken of in this recitation of the Prātimokṣa Sūtra, I now declare them.
Bestowed upon all sentient beings, may they together attain the Buddha-way.
